topic: The Soil Food Web Foundation turns 1
caption:
One year ago today, we became a nonprofit. Look what we built together. 💚
The Soil Food Web Foundation turns one today! When we filed as a 501(c)(3) a year ago, our mission was clear: bring healthy living soil to every ecoregion on this planet, and make the education to get there accessible to every farmer, gardener, and consultant who is ready to do the work.
Three hundred and sixty-five days later, we are still standing in that mission. And we were as busy as a ciliate on a mission to consume an aggregate of its favorite bacteria!
Honoring Dr. Elaine 💜
 🌸 We updated our logo to include purple flowers in her honor. Purple was her favorite color. With her passing, this year carried a weight we did not anticipate, and everything we do from here carries her legacy forward in the spirit she built it.
Making the education more accessible
 🎓 Awarded more than $300,000 in scholarships
 🎙️ Hosted 35 free live events
 🌎 Released our first Spanish-transcribed course, the Compost Intensive Course, opening the door for a whole new community of Spanish-speaking learners
Building better programs and support
 💻 Overhauled the learning management system for smoother navigation and a more personalized student experience
 📱 Launched a mobile app, so learners can access programs wherever they are
 🔬 Updated the Microbe Library with easier navigation, richer conversation, and the ability for students to contribute their own discoveries
 🎓 Completely restructured Advanced Programs with self-paced video learning so time with mentors goes toward real refinement of skills
 ⏳ Cut access limitations and expiration dates back significantly, so more students benefit from extended program access
 🌱 Launched the Compost Intensive Course as a cohort-based program open to anyone, no prerequisites required
Strengthening our communications
 🌐 Launched a new website
 📧 Moved to a new email support platform built for reliability and faster turnaround
 📰 Now publishing regular newsletters packed with education, community updates, and easy access to programs
 📅 Events calendar now forecasted a full year in advance
Growing meaningful partnerships
 🤝 Isha Outreach
 🤝 Hiwassee
 🤝 Navdanya, the organization founded by Vandana Shiva
 🌿 Launched a Permaculture Design Certificate in partnership with the Permaculture Alliance
Building real community
 👐 Released a free public community open to everyone
 🇺🇸 Held our first workshop on U.S. soil
 🇮🇳 Holding our first workshop in India
 🎤 Brought some of the most respected voices in regenerative agriculture into conversation with our community: Vandana Shiva, Geoff Lawton, Nicole Masters, Celine Bassett, Mary Reynolds, Clea Chandmal, and David Holmgren
We know that inoculant-grade biological amendments are the solution to many of the most pressing problems facing agriculture and the planet right now. 

This list of work is astounding, and we’ve likely forgotten a few things along the way. We cannot slow down, and we do not intend to.
None of this happens without our students, graduates, teaching team, partners, and donors. Thank you for growing with us. 🌱

topic: What can I do right now to improve my soil?
caption:
One of the questions we get most often is a simple one. What can I actually do right now to improve the soil near me?
We love this question because the answer is more accessible than most people expect.
Cover your soil first. Bare ground loses biology, moisture, and structure faster than most people realize, and the fix is as simple as mulch, cover crops, or even leaving leaf litter where it falls. Give the organisms below something to work with and they will.
Add biologically active compost to reintroduce the community that makes nutrient cycling possible: bacteria, fungi, protozoa, nematodes, all working together the way they are supposed to. If you can make it yourself, even better. If you are sourcing it, know what is actually in it.
Reduce tillage where you can. Fungal networks that took months to build can be gone in a single pass, and those networks are the architecture everything else depends on.
Feed those fungi. Woody mulch and carbon-rich organic material shift the fungal-to-bacterial balance toward resilience and long-term productivity.
And then tell someone what you are learning. Demonstration is still the most powerful thing we have. Anyone who sees healthy soil working and understands why might carry it forward somewhere new. 🌍
What is the first thing you did that made a visible difference in your soil? Share it below. 👇

topic: World Earthworm Day
caption:
Is World Earthworm Day even a thing? 🪱
Yes, it's real. In 2016, the Earthworm Society of Britain nominated 21 October as World Earthworm Day, and they chose October to honor Charles Darwin, since his worm book was published that month.
So let's celebrate the worm holes. Deep-burrowing earthworms dig vertical channels a meter or more into the soil and line them with nutrient-rich casts. Those burrows work as plumbing: rain soaks in fast, and roots follow them down into the subsoil. Every time you dig, you cut the pipes.
📤 Send this to the gardener who still digs every spring.
#WorldEarthwormDay #EarthwormsAreImportant #NoDig #SoilFoodWeb
words: Slide 1: "How do worms work their magic?"
Slide 2: Anecic earthworms dig vertical burrows that can reach 1 to 2 meters deep to break up compaction.
Slide 3: They spread microbes around as they move by lining the walls with mucus and casts, rich in nutrients and microbes.
Slide 4: Their channels let rain soak in fast without causing the ground to go anaerobic.
Slide 5: How to care for them?
Slide 6: Digging cuts the burrows. No-dig keeps the plumbing intact.
Slide 7: Add organic matter (Or simply don’t remove it)

topic: Soil Regenerators in the wild: Christina Olivero
caption:
This one makes our hearts full. 💚
Four years ago, Christina Olivero was working in advertising. Today she runs Alter Eco Farms, a soil regeneration business in Chattanooga, Tennessee.
It all started with one free Soil Food Web School webinar on protozoa. Christina came in with a lifelong love of biology and very little farming experience, and she kept going. Now she teaches workshops, sells biological amendments and runs soil tests, with trials across garden beds, pastures and aquaponics farms.
What we love most is how her whole community has gotten behind her, from farmers and gardeners to neighbors and city officials.
Christina, we are so proud of what you have built. Congratulations on finishing your final project, and we can't wait to see your consulting work grow!

topic: International Day of Climate Action: leave the leaves
caption:
Before you rake and bag those leaves this fall, read this! 🍂
Fallen leaves are one of the best gifts your soil gets all year. They are full of carbon and lignin, and fungi are the ones that break lignin down. When you leave the leaves, you are feeding the fungi that perennials, shrubs and trees depend on.
A layer of leaves also protects the soil over winter, and the residues fungi leave behind help build the stable carbon that stays in the ground.
On International Day of Climate Action, this is a simple change anyone can make. If you have a lawn, shred the leaves and move them onto your garden beds instead.
#ClimateAction #LeaveTheLeaves #SoilFoodWeb #LivingSoil #SoilHealth #SoilCarbon #Fungi #Mulch #FallGarden

Slide 2: Leaf litter is rich in carbon and lignin.
Slide 3: Fungi are the main decomposers of lignin.
Slide 4: That feeds the fungal soils trees and shrubs prefer.
Slide 5: A litter layer shields the soil over winter.
Slide 6: On lawns: shred the leaves and move them to your beds.

topic: Costa Rica: why we make compost together
caption:
Ready to take what you learned online into your hands? 🌿

topic: Soil Regenerators in the wild: Jason Gearheart
caption:
Meet Jason Gearheart, a Soil Food Web consultant in Indiana who turned woodchips into a growing compost business! 🚜
While he was training with us, Jason started his own company, Integrated Elements Compost, and got his facility certified by the Indiana Department of Environmental Management. He makes biologically active compost from woodchips, makes worm compost and his own blends of compost and castings, and sells it in paper bags, in bulk loads, in three local shops and at farmers markets.
Last year he made 120 yards of living compost. This year he is at 135 yards and counting. He even went back to school for a master's in environmental sustainability!
Jason, we are so proud of you and the quality you put into every batch. 💚
If you are in Indiana, get your compost at iecompost.com.

topic: Halloween: the vampire amoeba
caption:
Happy Halloween from the soil! 🧛
Meet the vampire amoeba. Vampyrellids are predatory amoebae that attach to algae and fungi, drill through the cell wall and drain what is inside. Some researchers are even studying them as natural predators of fungal plant diseases.
Our mentor Wes Sander wrote all about them on our blog, and it is the perfect spooky read for tonight. Link in bio.

topic: Inside a compost pile, day by day
caption:
Ever wondered what is happening inside your compost pile? 🔥
In a thermophilic compost pile, bacteria multiply fast in the first days and the pile heats up. That heat kills weed seeds and pathogens. When you turn the pile, you bring oxygen back in so it stays aerobic. As it cools, fungi and protozoa move in, and that is when your compost really comes alive.
Getting this right is a skill, and it is exactly what our Compost Intensive teaches you, step by step, alongside a group of fellow students. It starts January 18. Link in bio.
#Compost #ThermophilicCompost #SoilFoodWeb #SoilFoodWebSchool #LivingSoil #SoilHealth #SoilBiology #RegenerativeAgriculture

topic: Soil in numbers: the most common animal on Earth
caption:
Did you know the most common animal on Earth lives under your feet? 🪱
A study published in Nature in 2019 estimated there are about 440,000,000,000,000,000,000 nematodes in the world's soils. That is around 57 billion for every person alive!
Most of them eat bacteria and fungi, and when they do, they release nitrogen in a form plant roots can take up. They are a big part of how living soil feeds your plants.
#SoilInNumbers #Nematodes #SoilFoodWeb #SoilBiology #SoilMicrobiology #LivingSoil #SoilHealth
